claims.evidence: This is supported by in vivo data in Figure 5B showing limited effects of CDK inhibition alone.

claims.claim: Ime2-inhibition only caused limited Mcm2-7 reloading.
claims.source: Similar to CDK, however, Ime2-inhibition only caused limited Mcm2–7 reloading, although it did promote more significant reaccumulation of CDC6 mRNA and protein than CDK-inhibition (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vivo data in Figure 5C showing limited effects of Ime2 inhibition alone.

claims.claim: Neither CDK nor Ime2 are solely responsible for inhibiting helicase loading during the MI-MII transition.
claims.source: Therefore, neither CDK nor Ime2 are solely responsible for inhibiting helicase loading during the MI–MII transition.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that inhibition of either kinase alone does not cause robust helicase reloading.

claims.claim: Simultaneous inhibition of both CDK and Ime2 at the end of MI resulted in much higher levels of Mcm2-7 reloading than with either kinase alone.
claims.source: Strikingly, simultaneous inhibition of both CDK and Ime2 at the end of MI resulted in much higher levels of Mcm2–7 reloading than we observe with either kinase alone (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vivo data in Figure 5D showing robust helicase reloading upon co-inhibition.

claims.claim: Co-inhibition of CDK and Ime2 restored expression of CDC6 mRNA and protein to levels observed in pre-meiotic G1 cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, co–inhibition of these kinases restored expression of CDC6 mRNA and protein to levels observed in pre–meiotic G1 cells (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and northern blot data in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Ime2 phosphorylates multiple sites on Cdc6 within its phosphorylation-responsive degron domains in vitro.
claims.source: Consistent with repression of Cdc6 by both kinases, mass spectrometry analysis showed that Ime2 phosphorylates multiple sites on Cdc6 within its phosphorylation–responsive degron domains in vitro, and two of these sites directly overlap with CDK–sites known to contribute to Cdc6 degradation (Figure 5E, Supplementary file 1) (Calzada et al., 2000; Drury et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5E and Supplementary file 1, and cited references (Calzada et al., 2000; Drury et al., 2000).

claims.claim: Two Ime2 phosphorylation sites on Cdc6 directly overlap with CDK-sites known to contribute to Cdc6 degradation.
claims.source: Consistent with repression of Cdc6 by both kinases, mass spectrometry analysis showed that Ime2 phosphorylates multiple sites on Cdc6 within its phosphorylation–responsive degron domains in vitro, and two of these sites directly overlap with CDK–sites known to contribute to Cdc6 degradation (Figure 5E, Supplementary file 1) (Calzada et al., 2000; Drury et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data and cited references (Calzada et al., 2000; Drury et al., 2000).

claims.claim: Neither CDK nor Ime2 is capable of full inhibition of helicase loading but together they are a potent inhibitor of origin licensing and CDC6 expression during the MI-MII transition.
claims.source: Thus, neither CDK nor Ime2 is capable of full inhibition of helicase loading but together they are a potent inhibitor of origin licensing and CDC6 expression during the MI–MII transition.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined in vivo and in vitro data showing cooperative inhibition by both kinases.

claims.claim: Most helicase-activation proteins were present throughout the meiotic divisions, including Cdc45, Psf2, Sld3, and Dpb11.
claims.source: Most helicase–activation proteins were present throughout the meiotic divisions, including Cdc45, Psf2 (a member of the GINS complex), Sld3, and Dpb11 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Sld2 was robustly degraded upon entry into MI and did not reaccumulate until the completion of MII.
claims.source: In contrast, Sld2 was robustly degraded upon entry into MI and did not reaccumulate until the completion of MII (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Sld2 is required to form the active eukaryotic replicative helicase, the Cdc45-Mcm2-7-GINS (CMG) complex.
claims.source: Although helicase loading is an earlier event in replication initiation, we note that Sld2 is required to form the active eukaryotic replicative helicase, the Cdc45–Mcm2–7–GINS (CMG) complex (Heller et al., 2011; Kamimura et al., 1998; Muramatsu et al., 2010; Yeeles et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by multiple citations (Heller et al., 2011; Kamimura et al., 1998; Muramatsu et al., 2010; Yeeles et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Mutation of either Cdc5-phosphorylation sites or CDK-phosphorylation sites on Sld2 results in stabilization of Sld2 throughout the meiotic divisions.
claims.source: Mutation of either Cdc5–phosphorylation sites (sld2-2TA = T122A and T143A), CDK–phosphorylation sites (sld2-2SA = S128A and S138A), or both together (sld2-4A) resulted in stabilization of Sld2 during the meiotic divisions (Figure 6B–D, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6B-D.

claims.claim: Both CDK- and Cdc5-phosphorylation are required to drive substantial Sld2 degradation.
claims.source: Because both Sld2-2SA or Sld2-2TA were expressed at much higher levels than the WT protein during the meiotic divisions, both CDK– and Cdc5–phosphorylation are required to drive substantial Sld2 degradation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the levels of different Sld2 mutants in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: CDK and Cdc5 inhibit Mcm2-7 activation during the meiotic divisions by promoting Sld2 degradation.
claims.source: Together, these data indicate that CDK and Cdc5 inhibit Mcm2–7 activation during the meiotic divisions by promoting Sld2 degradation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing Sld2 degradation depends on CDK and Cdc5 phosphorylation sites.

claims.claim: If an origin escapes the inhibition of Mcm2-7 loading during the meiotic divisions, Sld2 degradation would prevent activation of the associated helicases.
claims.source: Thus, if an origin escapes the inhibition of Mcm2-7 loading during the meiotic divisions, Sld2 degradation would prevent activation of the associated helicases.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional consequence of Sld2 degradation.

claims.claim: Meiotic cells prevent DNA replication between the meiotic divisions using CDK, Ime2, and Cdc5 to inhibit both helicase loading and activation.
claims.source: In this study, we address a fundamental question concerning the regulation of meiosis; how do meiotic cells undergo two sequential rounds of chromosome segregation without an intervening S–phase? We found that meiotic cells prevent DNA replication between the meiotic divisions using CDK, Ime2, and Cdc5 to inhibit both helicase loading and activation.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: Ime2 and CDK cooperate to inhibit helicase loading, and their co-inhibition was sufficient for aberrant origin licensing during the MI-MII transition.
claims.source: Ime2 and CDK cooperate to inhibit helicase loading, and their co–inhibition was sufficient for aberrant origin licensing during the MI–MII transition.
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vivo data in Figure 5D showing robust helicase reloading upon co-inhibition.

claims.claim: Unlike CDK, Ime2 phosphorylation of Mcm2-7 directly inhibits its participation in helicase loading.
claims.source: In particular, we found that unlike CDK, Ime2 phosphorylation of Mcm2–7 directly inhibits its participation in helicase loading.
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro data in Figure 4 showing Ime2 phosphorylation of Mcm2-7 inhibits helicase loading.

claims.claim: Meiotic cells use CDK and the polo-like kinase Cdc5 to promote degradation of Sld2.
claims.source: In addition to the inhibition of origin licensing, meiotic cells use CDK and the polo–like kinase Cdc5 to promote degradation of Sld2, a key helicase-activation protein.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6 showing Sld2 degradation depends on CDK and Cdc5 phosphorylation sites.

claims.claim: Multiple kinases inhibit DNA replication between the two meiotic divisions by targeting both many components of the helicase-loading machinery and at least one helicase-activation protein.
claims.source: Together, these data reveal that multiple kinases inhibit DNA replication between the two meiotic divisions by targeting both many components of the helicase-loading machinery and at least one helicase-activation protein.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claims.claim: The amount of CDK activity present during the MI-MII transition is sufficient to inhibit most origin licensing.
claims.source: In support of the CDK–balance model, the amount of CDK activity present during the MI–MII transition is sufficient to inhibit most origin licensing, because Ime2 inhibition does not result in strong Mcm2–7 reloading.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that Ime2 inhibition alone does not cause robust helicase reloading.

claims.claim: The decrease in CDK activity that resets the chromosome segregation program is not sufficient to fully reset the DNA replication program.
claims.source: Thus, the decrease in CDK activity that resets the chromosome segregation program (Bizzari and Marston, 2011; Buonomo et al., 2003; Carlile and Amon, 2008; Fox et al., 2017; Marston et al., 2003) is not sufficient to fully reset the DNA replication program.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data and supported by multiple citations (Bizzari and Marston, 2011; Buonomo et al., 2003; Carlile and Amon, 2008; Fox et al., 2017; Marston et al., 2003).

claims.claim: CDK inhibition did not result in extensive Mcm2-7 reloading during the MI-MII transition.
claims.source: In support of the alternative–kinase model, we found that CDK inhibition similarly did not result in extensive Mcm2–7 reloading during the MI-MII transition.
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vivo data in Figure 5B showing limited effects of CDK inhibition alone.

claims.claim: Two additional kinases contribute to the inhibition of DNA replication between the meiotic divisions: Ime2 inhibits helicase loading, and Cdc5 helps stimulate the degradation of Sld2.
claims.source: Instead, we show that two additional kinases contribute to the inhibition of DNA replication between the meiotic divisions. Ime2 inhibits helicase loading, and Cdc5 helps stimulate the degradation of Sld2.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by the experimental data.

claims.claim: The inhibition of DNA replication by Ime2 and Cdc5 allows for CDK to oscillate and reset the chromosome segregation program without allowing a new round of DNA replication.
claims.source: The inhibition of DNA replication by Ime2 and Cdc5 allows for CDK to oscillate and reset the chromosome segregation program without allowing a new round of DNA replication.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claims.claim: Meiotic cells use Ime2 and Cdc5 to inhibit helicase loading and activation, respectively, suggesting that CDK-dependent inhibition of origin licensing is not adequate to ensure genome stability during meiosis.
claims.source: That meiotic cells use Ime2 and Cdc5 to inhibit helicase loading and activation, respectively, suggests that CDK–dependent inhibition of origin licensing is not adequate to ensure genome stability during meiosis.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings that multiple kinases are required.

claims.claim: A subset of the mechanisms by which CDK and Ime2 inhibit helicase loading are non-overlapping.
claims.source: Furthermore, a subset of the mechanisms by which CDK and Ime2 inhibit helicase loading are non–overlapping, providing additional avenues to prevent inappropriate replication (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4 showing different targets for CDK (ORC) and Ime2 (Mcm2-7).

claims.claim: The transient weakening of both Cdc6 repression and ORC phosphorylation during the MI-MII transition indicates that the associated decrease in CDK activity is a significant threat to origin licensing.
claims.source: The transient weakening of both Cdc6 repression and ORC phosphorylation during the MI–MII transition (Figure 2) indicates that the associated decrease in CDK activity (Carlile and Amon, 2008) is a significant threat to origin licensing.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 2 and cited reference (Carlile and Amon, 2008).

claims.claim: Ime2 has a larger role than CDK for Cdc6 repression at the MI-MII transition.
claims.source: Even the additional repression of Cdc6 by Ime2 is not sufficient to fully eliminate the protein during the MI-MII transition, although Ime2 has a larger role than CDK for Cdc6 repression at this time (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the effects of CDK and Ime2 inhibition on Cdc6 levels in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Preventing DNA re-replication in meiotic cells is more important than in mitotic cells to ensure that the inherited genome remains intact in multicellular eukaryotes.
claims.source: It is worth noting that in multicellular eukaryotes, preventing DNA re-replication in meiotic cells is more important than in mitotic cells to ensure that the inherited genome remains intact.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of preventing re-replication in meiosis.

claims.claim: In mitotic cells, prevention of DNA re-replication relies on inhibiting Mcm2-7 loading.
claims.source: In mitotic cells, prevention of DNA re–replication relies on inhibiting Mcm2–7 loading (Arias and Walter, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation (Arias and Walter, 2007).

claims.claim: Sld2 degradation in mitotic cells is important for ensuring genome stability at the M-G1 transition, but not during other parts of the mitotic cell cycle.
claims.source: Previous studies found that Sld2 degradation in mitotic cells is important for ensuring genome stability at the M–G1 transition, but not during other parts of the mitotic cell cycle (Reusswig et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation (Reusswig et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Mechanisms preventing DNA re-replication at the mitotic M-G1 transition also function during meiosis at the MI-MII transition.
claims.source: Our finding that Sld2 is absent during both meiotic divisions suggests that mechanisms preventing DNA re–replication at the mitotic M–G1 transition also function during meiosis at the MI–MII transition, a partially G1-like state.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that Sld2 is degraded during meiotic divisions.

claims.claim: Dbf4 is degraded during both mitotic anaphase and meiotic anaphase I.
claims.source: Consistent with this idea, Dbf4, which binds to Cdc7 to form the kinase DDK and is also required for helicase activation, is degraded during both mitotic anaphase (Ferreira et al., 2000) as well as meiotic anaphase I (Matos et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Ferreira et al., 2000; Matos et al., 2008).

claims.claim: The degradation of Sld2 and Dbf4 strongly suggests that meiotic cells further protect themselves from replication initiation during the meiotic divisions by inhibiting multiple steps during Mcm2-7 activation.
claims.source: The degradation of these two proteins strongly suggests that meiotic cells further protect themselves from replication initiation during the meiotic divisions by inhibiting multiple steps during Mcm2–7 activation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that multiple helicase activation proteins are degraded.

claims.claim: Ime2 is not just a backup for the known inhibitory mechanisms used by CDK.
claims.source: Ime2 is not just a backup for the known inhibitory mechanisms used by CDK.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that Ime2 has distinct mechanisms of inhibition compared to CDK.

claims.claim: Ime2 uses at least two mechanisms similar to CDK: Cdc6 degradation and Mcm2-7 nuclear export.
claims.source: We found that in addition to using at least two mechanisms similar to CDK (Cdc6 degradation (Figure 5) (Drury et al., 2000) and Mcm2-7 nuclear export (Holt et al., 2007)), Ime2-phosphorylation of Mcm2-7 results in a distinct mechanism of inhibition not seen after CDK-phosphorylation (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figures 4 and 5, and citations (Drury et al., 2000; Holt et al., 2007).

claims.claim: Ime2-phosphorylation of Mcm2-7 results in a distinct mechanism of inhibition not seen after CDK-phosphorylation.
claims.source: We found that in addition to using at least two mechanisms similar to CDK (Cdc6 degradation (Figure 5) (Drury et al., 2000) and Mcm2-7 nuclear export (Holt et al., 2007)), Ime2-phosphorylation of Mcm2-7 results in a distinct mechanism of inhibition not seen after CDK-phosphorylation (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4 showing Ime2 targets Mcm2-7 while CDK targets ORC.

claims.claim: Previous studies have not identified a mechanism that directly prevents Mcm2-7 from completing helicase loading.
claims.source: Origin licensing is inhibited by a number of different mechanisms across eukaryotic evolution, but previous studies have not identified a mechanism that directly prevents Mcm2-7 from completing helicase loading (Arias and Walter, 2007; Siddiqui et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Arias and Walter, 2007; Siddiqui et al., 2013).

claims.claim: The ability of Ime2 to inhibit helicase loading suggests an important role for this kinase during the meiotic G1-S transition.
claims.source: The ability of Ime2 to inhibit helicase loading also suggests an important role for this kinase during the meiotic G1–S transition.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings about Ime2's role in inhibiting helicase loading.

claims.claim: During the mitotic G1-S transition, helicase loading is inhibited by G1-CDK before helicase activation is stimulated by S-phase CDK.
claims.source: During the mitotic G1–S transition, helicase loading is inhibited by G1–CDK before helicase activation is stimulated by S–phase CDK (Drury et al., 2000; Labib et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Drury et al., 2000; Labib et al., 1999).

claims.claim: During meiosis, G1 cyclins are not expressed and it is Ime2 that triggers activation of S-CDK at the G1-S transition.
claims.source: During meiosis, G1 cyclins are not expressed and it is Ime2 that triggers activation of S–CDK at the G1–S transition (Benjamin et al., 2003; Dirick et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Benjamin et al., 2003; Dirick et al., 1998).

claims.claim: Ime2 can robustly inhibit helicase loading by multiple mechanisms, similar to G1-CDK.
claims.source: Our data and previous studies (Holt et al., 2007) show that Ime2 can robustly inhibit helicase loading by multiple mechanisms, similar to G1-CDK.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current data and cited previous study (Holt et al., 2007).

claims.claim: Ime2 insulates helicase loading from helicase activation during the meiotic G1-S transition in an analogous manner to G1-CDK during the mitotic G1-S transition.
claims.source: These observations strongly suggest that Ime2 insulates helicase loading from helicase activation during the meiotic G1–S transition in an analogous manner to G1–CDK during the mitotic G1–S transition.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of Ime2's role in meiosis to G1-CDK's role in mitosis.

claims.claim: The problem of uncoupling DNA replication and chromosome segregation during meiosis is conserved in other eukaryotes.
claims.source: The problem of uncoupling DNA replication and chromosome segregation during meiosis is conserved in other eukaryotes.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about the conservation of this biological problem.

claims.claim: Metazoans also use CDK to regulate both chromosome segregation and DNA replication.
claims.source: Metazoans also use CDK to regulate both chromosome segregation and DNA replication (Arias and Walter, 2007; Malumbres and Barbacid, 2009; Siddiqui et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Arias and Walter, 2007; Malumbres and Barbacid, 2009; Siddiqui et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Metazoans mostly rely on CDK-independent mechanisms to inhibit Mcm2-7 loading during S and G2 phase.
claims.source: Although metazoans mostly rely on CDK–independent mechanisms to inhibit Mcm2–7 loading during S and G2 phase, these mechanisms are not as potent during M–phase at which point Cdk1 becomes a critical inhibitor of origin licensing (Arias and Walter, 2007; Siddiqui et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Arias and Walter, 2007; Siddiqui et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Cdk1 becomes a critical inhibitor of origin licensing during M-phase in metazoans.
claims.source: Although metazoans mostly rely on CDK–independent mechanisms to inhibit Mcm2–7 loading during S and G2 phase, these mechanisms are not as potent during M–phase at which point Cdk1 becomes a critical inhibitor of origin licensing (Arias and Walter, 2007; Siddiqui et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Arias and Walter, 2007; Siddiqui et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Transient inactivation of Cdk1 in human cells is sufficient for DNA re-replication, just as it is in yeast.
claims.source: Transient inactivation of Cdk1 in human cells is sufficient for DNA re–replication, just as it is in yeast (Bates et al., 1998; Dahmann et al., 1995; Itzhaki et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Bates et al., 1998; Dahmann et al., 1995; Itzhaki et al., 1997).

claims.claim: An oscillation of Cdk1 activity is required for correct chromosome segregation in mammalian cells.
claims.source: An oscillation of Cdk1 activity is also required for correct chromosome segregation in mammalian cells (Malumbres and Barbacid, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation (Malumbres and Barbacid, 2009).

claims.claim: Human Cdk2 can rescue some meiotic defects associated with ime2∆ in yeast.
claims.source: Human Cdk2 can rescue some meiotic defects associated with ime2∆ in yeast (Szwarcwort-Cohen et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation (Szwarcwort-Cohen et al., 2009).

claims.claim: Cdk2 is not required for mitosis in mice, but it is required for both male and female meiosis.
claims.source: Additionally, Cdk2 is not required for mitosis in mice, but it is required for both male and female meiosis (Ortega et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation (Ortega et al., 2003).

claims.claim: Mammalian Cdk2 may have a similar role during meiosis as Ime2 does in yeast.
claims.source: With regard to how DNA replication and chromosome segregation are uncoupled during mammalian meiosis, previous studies raise the intriguing possibility that mammalian Cdk2 may have a similar role during meiosis as Ime2 does in yeast.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the cited studies about Cdk2 and Ime2.

claims.claim: During G1 phase, low CDK activity allows for the Mcm2-7 complex to be loaded onto origins of replication in an inactive state.
claims.source: During G1 phase, low CDK activity allows for the Mcm2–7 complex, the core enzyme of the replicative helicase, to be loaded onto origins of replication in an inactive state.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the mitotic cell cycle regulation stated in the introduction.

claims.claim: Helicase loading cannot occur in the presence of high CDK activity.
claims.source: This event, known as origin licensing or helicase loading, cannot occur in the presence of high CDK activity and requires the cooperative action of three proteins: Cdc6, Cdt1, and the Origin Recognition Complex (ORC) (Evrin et al., 2009; Remus et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Evrin et al., 2009; Remus et al., 2009).

claims.claim: Helicase loading requires the cooperative action of three proteins: Cdc6, Cdt1, and the Origin Recognition Complex (ORC).
claims.source: This event, known as origin licensing or helicase loading, cannot occur in the presence of high CDK activity and requires the cooperative action of three proteins: Cdc6, Cdt1, and the Origin Recognition Complex (ORC) (Evrin et al., 2009; Remus et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Evrin et al., 2009; Remus et al., 2009).

claims.claim: S-CDK phosphorylates Sld2 and Sld3 to promote helicase activation, replisome assembly, and chromosome duplication.
claims.source: Upon S–phase entry, S–CDK (CDK bound to S-phase cyclins Clb5/6) is activated and impacts DNA replication in two ways. First, S–CDK phosphorylates two essential proteins, Sld2 and Sld3, that subsequently promote helicase activation, replisome assembly, and chromosome duplication (Masumoto et al., 2002; Tanaka et al., 2007; Zegerman and Diffley, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Masumoto et al., 2002; Tanaka et al., 2007; Zegerman and Diffley, 2007).

claims.claim: Both S-CDK and M-CDK inhibit new helicase loading during S, G2, and M phases.
claims.source: Second, both S–CDK and M-CDK (CDK bound to mitotic cyclins Clb1-4) inhibit new helicase loading during S, G2, and M phases.
claims.evidence: This is a description of CDK regulation stated in the introduction.

claims.claim: CDK directly phosphorylates Cdc6, Mcm3, and ORC to trigger the proteolytic degradation of Cdc6, the nuclear export of Mcm2-7-Cdt1, and inhibition of ORC helicase-loading activity.
claims.source: These kinases directly phosphorylate Cdc6, Mcm3, and ORC to trigger the proteolytic degradation of Cdc6, the nuclear export of Mcm2–7–Cdt1, and inhibition of ORC helicase–loading activity, respectively (Calzada et al., 2000; Chen and Bell, 2011; Drury et al., 2000; Labib et al., 1999; Nguyen et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by multiple citations (Calzada et al., 2000; Chen and Bell, 2011; Drury et al., 2000; Labib et al., 1999; Nguyen et al., 2000).

claims.claim: CDK oscillations ensure that chromosome segregation occurs once per mitotic cell cycle.
claims.source: CDK oscillations also ensure that chromosome segregation occurs once per mitotic cell cycle (Winey and Bloom, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation (Winey and Bloom, 2012).

claims.claim: G1-CDK is required for duplication of the SPB at the end of G1 phase.
claims.source: At the end of G1 phase, G1–CDK (CDK bound to G1 cyclins Cln1-3) is required for duplication of the SPB (Jaspersen et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation (Jaspersen et al., 2004).

claims.claim: S-CDK and M-CDK prevent re-duplication of SPBs.
claims.source: Later in the cell cycle, S–CDK and M–CDK prevent re–duplication of SPBs, and M-CDK is essential for the assembly of metaphase spindles (Avena et al., 2014; Elserafy et al., 2014; Haase et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Avena et al., 2014; Elserafy et al., 2014; Haase et al., 2001).

claims.claim: M-CDK is essential for the assembly of metaphase spindles.
claims.source: Later in the cell cycle, S–CDK and M–CDK prevent re–duplication of SPBs, and M-CDK is essential for the assembly of metaphase spindles (Avena et al., 2014; Elserafy et al., 2014; Haase et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Avena et al., 2014; Elserafy et al., 2014; Haase et al., 2001).

claims.claim: Downregulation of CDK activity is required for anaphase spindle disassembly upon completion of chromosome segregation.
claims.source: Finally, downregulation of CDK activity is required for anaphase spindle disassembly upon completion of chromosome segregation (Shirayama et al., 1999; Thornton and Toczyski, 2003; Wäsch and Cross, 2002).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Shirayama et al., 1999; Thornton and Toczyski, 2003; Wäsch and Cross, 2002).

claims.claim: The CDK-balance model suggests that partially inactivating CDK is sufficient to reset the chromosome segregation program while still inhibiting Mcm2-7 loading and replication initiation.
claims.source: The CDK–balance model suggests that partially inactivating CDK is sufficient to reset the chromosome segregation program while still inhibiting Mcm2–7 loading and replication initiation (Iwabuchi et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is a description of a model stated in the introduction and supported by citation (Iwabuchi et al., 2000).

claims.claim: The alternative-kinase model suggests that a second kinase inhibits Mcm2-7 loading during the MI-MII transition.
claims.source: In contrast, the alternative–kinase model suggests that a second kinase inhibits Mcm2–7 loading during the MI–MII transition, allowing the oscillation of CDK activity to reset the chromosome segregation program without resetting the DNA replication program.
claims.evidence: This is a description of a model stated in the introduction.

claims.claim: Ime2 has been proposed to inhibit Mcm2-7 loading during the MI-MII transition.
claims.source: Ime2, a yeast meiosis–specific kinase that is evolutionarily related to CDK (Krylov et al., 2003), has been proposed to have this role (Holt et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Krylov et al., 2003; Holt et al., 2007).

claims.claim: Ime2 is a yeast meiosis-specific kinase that is evolutionarily related to CDK.
claims.source: Ime2, a yeast meiosis–specific kinase that is evolutionarily related to CDK (Krylov et al., 2003), has been proposed to have this role (Holt et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation (Krylov et al., 2003).

claims.claim: Ime2 is active during the meiotic divisions.
claims.source: Previous studies found that Ime2 is active during the meiotic divisions (Berchowitz et al., 2013) and that, like CDK, this kinase can promote Mcm2–7 nuclear export upon completion of meiotic S phase (Holt et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation (Berchowitz et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Ime2 can promote Mcm2-7 nuclear export upon completion of meiotic S phase.
claims.source: Previous studies found that Ime2 is active during the meiotic divisions (Berchowitz et al., 2013) and that, like CDK, this kinase can promote Mcm2–7 nuclear export upon completion of meiotic S phase (Holt et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation (Holt et al., 2007).

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of Orc2 and Orc6 by CDK prevents ORC from facilitating helicase loading.
claims.source: Phosphorylation of Orc2 and Orc6 by CDK prevents ORC from facilitating helicase loading (Chen and Bell, 2011; Nguyen et al., 2001).

results.result: Mcm2-7 loading is inhibited during the MI-MII transition while ORC remains bound to origins. ORC binding was detected at multiple origins (ARS1, ARS1413, ARS305, ARS418) throughout both meiotic divisions, but Mcm2-7 was only present at origins during pre-meiotic G1 phase and did not reassociate during or between the meiotic divisions. This establishes Mcm2-7 loading as the earliest inhibited step of replisome assembly during the MI-MII transition.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C13 and C106-C109 are well-supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figures 1B and 1C, demonstrating persistent ORC binding and absence of Mcm2-7 loading during meiotic divisions. The data are internally consistent across multiple origins and include appropriate controls (non-origin DNA, protein abundance). The conclusion that Mcm2-7 loading is the earliest inhibited step is logically derived from these observations.

results.result: CDK-dependent mechanisms inhibiting Mcm2-7 loading are transiently weakened during the MI-MII transition. Orc2 and Orc6 showed partial dephosphorylation at the MI-MII transition, and Cdc6 protein and mRNA partially reaccumulated during this period, indicating that reduced CDK activity during the MI-MII transition results in weakening of at least two CDK-dependent inhibitory mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C19 and C103-C105 are supported by immunoblot and northern blot data in Figure 2 showing transient changes in ORC phosphorylation and Cdc6 levels. The data demonstrate clear mobility shifts for Orc2/Orc6 and protein/mRNA reaccumulation for Cdc6 at the MI-MII transition. The conclusion that CDK-dependent mechanisms are weakened is well-supported by these observations and consistent with known CDK activity changes.

results.result: Ime2 directly inhibits helicase loading through phosphorylation of helicase-loading proteins. Pre-treatment of purified helicase-loading proteins with Ime2 fully inhibited Mcm2-7 loading in vitro, and this inhibition required Ime2 kinase activity as demonstrated by analog-sensitive Ime2 experiments. Ime2 phosphorylation does not block OCCM complex formation, indicating it inhibits a downstream step after initial Mcm2-7 recruitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C23 and C104 are strongly supported by in vitro reconstitution experiments in Figure 3. The use of purified proteins demonstrates direct inhibition, the analog-sensitive kinase approach with 1-NA-PP1 confirms kinase activity dependence, and the OCCM formation assay identifies the step inhibited. The experimental design is rigorous and the conclusions are well-justified.

results.result: Ime2 phosphorylation of Mcm2-7 is the primary mechanism by which Ime2 inhibits helicase loading, distinct from CDK. In vitro kinase assays showed Ime2 phosphorylates multiple helicase-loading proteins, but selective phosphorylation experiments revealed that Mcm2-7 phosphorylation alone caused >90% inhibition of helicase loading, while ORC phosphorylation caused ~50% inhibition. In contrast, CDK primarily targets ORC, demonstrating non-overlapping mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C29, C47, C56, and C67 are well-supported by systematic in vitro experiments in Figure 4 that individually phosphorylate each helicase-loading protein. The quantification (Figure 4C) shows clear differences in inhibition levels, and comparison with CDK (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) demonstrates distinct targets. The experimental design effectively isolates the contribution of each phosphorylation target.

results.result: CDK and Ime2 cooperatively inhibit helicase loading during the MI-MII transition. Inhibition of either CDK or Ime2 alone at the end of MI caused only limited Mcm2-7 reloading, but simultaneous inhibition of both kinases resulted in much higher levels of Mcm2-7 reloading and restored CDC6 mRNA and protein expression to G1 levels, demonstrating that neither kinase alone is sufficient but together they potently inhibit origin licensing.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3, C30-C34, C37, C46, and C52 are strongly supported by in vivo experiments in Figure 5 using analog-sensitive alleles. The data clearly show synergistic effects of co-inhibition on Mcm2-7 loading, Cdc6 levels, and ORC phosphorylation. The experimental design with all four genotype combinations (WT, cdk1-as, ime2-as, double mutant) provides compelling evidence for cooperative inhibition.

results.result: Ime2 phosphorylates Cdc6 at sites overlapping with CDK phosphorylation sites in degron domains. Mass spectrometry analysis showed Ime2 phosphorylates multiple sites on Cdc6 within phosphorylation-responsive degron domains, with two sites directly overlapping CDK sites known to contribute to Cdc6 degradation, and Ime2 has a larger role than CDK for Cdc6 repression at the MI-MII transition.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 and C58 are supported by iTRAQ LC-MS/MS data in Figure 5E and Supplementary file 1, showing specific phosphorylation sites. The overlap with known CDK sites is documented in prior literature (Calzada et al., 2000; Drury et al., 2000). The conclusion about Ime2's larger role is supported by comparing effects of CDK vs Ime2 inhibition on Cdc6 levels in Figure 5.

results.result: CDK and Cdc5 promote degradation of Sld2 during the meiotic divisions. While most helicase-activation proteins remained present throughout meiosis, Sld2 was robustly degraded upon entry into MI and did not reaccumulate until completion of MII. Mutation of either Cdc5 or CDK phosphorylation sites on Sld2 resulted in protein stabilization, with both kinases required for substantial degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C38-C39, C41-C43, and C48 are well-supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6. The time course shows clear Sld2 degradation during meiotic divisions, and phosphorylation site mutants (2TA, 2SA, 4A) show stabilization. Quantification in Figure 6E demonstrates both kinases contribute to degradation. The experimental design with multiple mutants and quantification across cell cycle stages is rigorous.

results.result: Multiple kinases (CDK, Ime2, and Cdc5) inhibit both helicase loading and activation between the meiotic divisions to ensure reductive cell division. CDK and Ime2 cooperatively inhibit helicase loading through multiple mechanisms, while CDK and Cdc5 promote Sld2 degradation to inhibit helicase activation. This multi-layered inhibition allows CDK to oscillate and reset the chromosome segregation program without allowing DNA replication.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C45, C49, C53-C54 represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing results from all experimental approaches. These conclusions are well-supported by the collective data showing: (1) cooperative inhibition of helicase loading by CDK and Ime2 (Figure 5), (2) distinct mechanisms for each kinase (Figures 3-4), and (3) Sld2 degradation by CDK and Cdc5 (Figure 6). The integration of these findings provides a comprehensive model.

results.result: The amount of CDK activity during the MI-MII transition is sufficient to inhibit most origin licensing, but the decrease in CDK activity that resets chromosome segregation is not sufficient to fully reset the DNA replication program. The transient weakening of Cdc6 repression and ORC phosphorylation indicates that decreased CDK activity poses a significant threat to origin licensing, suggesting CDK-dependent inhibition alone is inadequate for genome stability during meiosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51, C55, and C57 are supported by the observation that Ime2 inhibition alone does not cause robust helicase reloading (Figure 5C), indicating sufficient CDK activity remains. The transient weakening of CDK-dependent mechanisms (Figure 2) combined with the requirement for multiple kinases (Figure 5D) supports the conclusion that CDK alone is insufficient. The reasoning is logically sound.

results.result: Ime2 is not merely a backup for CDK but uses both overlapping and distinct mechanisms to inhibit helicase loading. Ime2 uses at least two mechanisms similar to CDK (Cdc6 degradation and Mcm2-7 nuclear export) but also employs a distinct mechanism through direct phosphorylation of Mcm2-7 that prevents helicase loading completion—a mechanism not previously identified in studies of origin licensing inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66, C68, and C72 are supported by data showing Ime2 targets Mcm2-7 while CDK targets ORC (Figure 4), both kinases affect Cdc6 (Figure 5E), and prior work on nuclear export (Holt et al., 2007). The claim about novelty (C68) is supported by citations to comprehensive reviews (Arias and Walter, 2007; Siddiqui et al., 2013). The conclusion is well-justified.

results.result: Ime2 likely insulates helicase loading from helicase activation during the meiotic G1-S transition, analogous to G1-CDK in mitosis. During mitotic G1-S transition, G1-CDK inhibits helicase loading before S-CDK stimulates activation. During meiosis, G1 cyclins are not expressed and Ime2 triggers S-CDK activation, suggesting Ime2 performs the insulation function of G1-CDK.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 and C73 present a well-reasoned model based on the demonstrated ability of Ime2 to inhibit helicase loading by multiple mechanisms (current data) and established knowledge about cell cycle regulation (supported by citations: Benjamin et al., 2003; Dirick et al., 1998; Drury et al., 2000; Labib et al., 1999). The analogy is logical and supported by functional similarities.

results.result: Meiotic cells inhibit multiple steps of Mcm2-7 activation, similar to mechanisms at the mitotic M-G1 transition. Sld2 is required for CMG complex formation and is degraded during both meiotic divisions, similar to its degradation at the mitotic M-G1 transition. Dbf4, another helicase activation protein, is also degraded during both mitotic and meiotic anaphase, suggesting meiotic cells protect against replication initiation by inhibiting multiple activation steps.
results.evaluation: Claims C40, C60-C64 are supported by the Sld2 degradation data (Figure 6) and citations for Sld2 function (Heller et al., 2011; Kamimura et al., 1998; Muramatsu et al., 2010; Yeeles et al., 2015), mitotic Sld2 degradation (Reusswig et al., 2016), and Dbf4 degradation (Ferreira et al., 2000; Matos et al., 2008). The parallel between mitotic and meiotic mechanisms is well-supported.

results.result: The problem of uncoupling DNA replication and chromosome segregation during meiosis is conserved in metazoans, and mammalian Cdk2 may have a similar role to yeast Ime2. Metazoans use CDK to regulate both processes, with Cdk1 becoming critical for inhibiting origin licensing during M-phase. Human Cdk2 can rescue some ime2Δ meiotic defects in yeast, and Cdk2 is required for meiosis but not mitosis in mice, suggesting functional similarity to Ime2.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C82 are well-supported by multiple citations documenting CDK regulation in metazoans (Arias and Walter, 2007; Malumbres and Barbacid, 2009; Siddiqui et al., 2013), Cdk1 re-replication (Bates et al., 1998; Dahmann et al., 1995; Itzhaki et al., 1997), Cdk2 rescue of ime2Δ (Szwarcwort-Cohen et al., 2009), and Cdk2 meiotic requirement (Ortega et al., 2003). The speculation about Cdk2 function (C82) is appropriately qualified.

results.result: Background on meiosis, DNA replication, and cell cycle regulation. These claims establish the fundamental biology of meiosis (single DNA replication, two divisions), the role of CDK in regulating both DNA replication and chromosome segregation in mitotic cells, and the two competing models (CDK-balance vs. alternative-kinase) for how meiotic cells uncouple these processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C83-C102 provide essential background information supported by extensive citations to established literature. These are well-accepted facts about meiosis, DNA replication initiation, CDK regulation, and prior hypotheses. The claims accurately represent current knowledge and provide necessary context for the experimental work.

results.result: Speculative claims about the functional importance of the findings. If an origin escapes inhibition of Mcm2-7 loading, Sld2 degradation would prevent helicase activation. Preventing DNA re-replication in meiotic cells is more important than in mitotic cells for maintaining genome integrity in multicellular eukaryotes.
results.evaluation: Claims C44 and C59 are reasonable inferences from the data but are explicitly speculative. C44 logically follows from the demonstration that Sld2 is degraded and required for helicase activation. C59 is a general statement about the importance of germline genome integrity that is biologically reasonable but not directly tested. These are appropriately presented as interpretations rather than demonstrated facts.
